**Commentary of al-Mawardi (*al-Nukat wa al-'Uyun*) on Surah 96, verses 6–19:**

﴿Truly, man does transgress.﴾ Regarding *kalla* (no; nay) here there are two views:

First: it is a refutation and a denial. This is the view of al-Farra'.

Second: it means *illa* (except/but), and likewise *"Kullan sa-ya'lamun"* (Surah 78:4-5, "Nay, they will come to know"). This is the view of Abu Hatim al-Sijistani.

Regarding His words ﴿yatgha* (transgress)﴾ there are four views. The second: it means *layabtaru* (he becomes insolent and boastful). This is the view of al-Kalbi.

The third: it means he rises from one station to another. This is the view of al-Suddi.

The fourth: his rank exceeds its limit, and from this is His saying, ﴿Indeed, when the water rose beyond its bounds (*taghā al-mā'*)﴾ (69:11). This is the view of Ibn Shajara.

﴿When he sees himself self-sufficient.﴾ That is, self-sufficient of his Lord. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas.

It may also bear a second meaning: he is self-sufficient through his wealth and property. Al-Kalbi said: it was revealed concerning Abu Jahl.

﴿Indeed, to your Lord is the return.﴾ Regarding this there are two views:

First: the final end. This is the view of al-Dahhak.

Second: the return on the Day of Resurrection.

It may also bear a third meaning: Allah returns him to decline after perfection, and to death after life.

﴿Have you seen the one who forbids﴾ ﴿a servant when he prays?﴾ It was revealed concerning Abu Jahl. Abu Hurayrah narrated that Abu Jahl said: "By al-Lat and al-'Uzza, if I see Muhammad praying among you, I will surely trample his neck and rub his face in the dust." Then he came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while he was praying, intending to trample his neck. But suddenly he was seen (p-307) retreating, that is, going back on his heels. He was asked, "What is the matter with you?" He said: "Between me and him there is a trench of fire, and wind, and wings." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "If he had come near me, the angels would have snatched him limb from limb." Al-Hasan narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Every nation has a Pharaoh, and the Pharaoh of this nation is Abu Jahl." The prayer in which Abu Jahl intended to harm the Messenger of Allah was the Zuhr prayer.

Ja'far ibn Muhammad related that the first congregational prayer offered in Islam, which is likely to be the one Abu Jahl denied, was prayed by the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him). Abu Talib passed by them with his son Ja'far and said: "Join the wing of your cousin," and he went away joyful, saying:

> Indeed 'Ali and Ja'far are my trust in the times of calamity and distress.
> By Allah, I will not forsake the Prophet, nor will one of noble lineage forsake him.
> Do not forsake him, but support your cousin,
> My brother by my mother, from among their sons and my father.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) heard of this.

﴿Have you considered if he is upon guidance﴾ ﴿or enjoins righteousness?﴾ Regarding this there are two views:

First: it refers to Abu Jahl, and there is an implied element in it, its meaning being: "Would it not have been better for him?"

Second: it refers to the Prophet (ﷺ). He was upon guidance in himself, and he enjoined righteousness in obedience to his Lord.

Regarding His words "*Ara'ayta* (Have you considered)" there is the possibility of both views:

First: it is an address to the Prophet (ﷺ).

Second: it is a general address to him and to his community. The intended meaning in both views is his guidance, and in the speech there is an omitted element, its meaning being: "This is how He treated him."

﴿Have you considered if he denies and turns away?﴾ It refers to Abu Jahl, and regarding it there are two views:

First: he denied Allah and turned away from His obedience.

Second: he denied the Qur'an and turned away from faith.

It may also bear a third meaning: he denied the Messenger and turned away from accepting him.

(p-308)

﴿Does he not know that Allah sees?﴾ It refers to Abu Jahl, and regarding it there are two views:

First: "Do you not know, O Muhammad, that Allah sees Abu Jahl?"

Second: "Do you not know, O Abu Jahl, that Allah sees you?"

Regarding it there are two views:

First: He sees his deed and hears his speech.

Second: He sees you in your prayer when Abu Jahl forbade you from it.

It may also bear a third meaning: He sees what Abu Jahl intended, and so He does not enable him against His Messenger.

﴿Nay! If he does not desist, We will surely seize him by the forelock,﴾ referring to Abu Jahl. Regarding it there are two views:

First: it means "We will surely take him by his forelock." This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, and among the Arabs it is more forceful in conveying humiliation and disgrace. From this is the saying of al-Khansa':

> We cut the forelocks of their horsemen,
> and they used to think that they would never be cut.

Second: its meaning is the blackening of faces and the disfiguring of their form with a black mark, derived from their saying: "The fire or the sun has *safa'at* him" when it altered his face into a disfigured state. The poet said:

> Its three hearthstones blackened by the campsite of a cauldron,
> and its basin like the stump of a pool, not chipped.

The forelock (*nasiyah*) is the hair of the front of the head, and it may be used to refer to the whole of the person, as one says: "This is a blessed forelock," indicating the whole person.

Then He said: ﴿a lying, sinful forelock﴾, that is: the forelock of Abu Jahl is lying in its speech and sinful in its deeds.

﴿Then let him call his assembly﴾, referring to Abu Jahl. *Al-nadi* is the gathering of the people of generosity and munificence. The meaning of ﴿let him call his assembly﴾ is: let him call the people of his assembly, from among his tribe or his helpers.

﴿We will call the guardians (*al-zabaniyah*)﴾. *Al-zabaniyah* (the guardian angels of Hell, the keepers of Jahannam) are the angels who are the keepers of Hell; they are the greatest of the angels in creation and the most severe in seizing. The Arabs use this name for anyone who is severe in seizing. The poet said:

> Generous in the remote lands, spear-thrusters in battle,
> stern guardians, great, whose wisdom is… (*zabaniyah ghulb 'izam hulumuha*)

﴿Nay! Do not obey him﴾. Abu Hurayrah said: "Nay! Do not obey Abu Jahl in his command."

His prohibition against obeying him may bear two meanings:

First: do not accept his speech if he flatters you, nor his opinion if he approaches you.

Second: do not respond to his speech, and do not confront him in his deeds. From this is what is reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "O Allah, do not obey (i.e., do not answer the supplication of) a traveller among us—because the traveller supplicates for the cessation of rain; if his supplication were answered, the people would perish."

﴿And prostrate and draw near﴾. Regarding it there are two views:

First: prostrate, you, O Muhammad, in prayer, and draw near, you, O Abu Jahl, to the Fire. This is the view of Zayd ibn Aslam.

Second: prostrate, you, O Muhammad, in your prayer so that you may draw near to your Lord, for the closest a servant is to Allah the Exalted is when he prostrates to Him.

Juwaybir narrated from al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: Eighty-four verses were revealed concerning Abu Jahl, one hundred and four concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, and thirty-two concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith.
